subject: Cognitive Science
title: Texting While Driving
description: A micro-lesson that makes Texting While Driving usable.

hook.text: A driver texting for five seconds at highway speed crosses an entire football field blind.

buildup.text: Studies show texting impairs driving as much as being at the legal alcohol limit.

discovery.text: It's not just eyes off the road—it's mind off the road. Cognitive distraction is the real killer.

twist.text: Hands-free calling isn't much safer. The conversation itself steals attentional resources from driving.

climax.text: Passengers adjust talk during risky moments. A phone caller can't see the road, so they keep going.

punchline.text: The danger isn't the phone in your hand—it's the task in your head.

quiz.question: Why isn't hands-free calling much safer while driving?

details.summary: Texting while driving combines multiple attention-demanding tasks: visual, manual, and cognitive. Research shows it increases crash risk by up to 23 times and impairs driving performance more than alcohol intoxication. The brain simply cannot safely manage both tasks simultaneously.
details.whyItMatters: Texting while driving is one of the deadliest real-world consequences of attention limits. It kills thousands annually and demonstrates that no amount of practice makes true multitasking safe.
takeaways: Texting increases crash risk by up to 23 times
It impairs driving more than alcohol intoxication does
Eyes off the road for 5 seconds at highway speed covers a football field

faq.question: Why is texting more dangerous than talking on the phone while driving?
faq.answer: Texting demands visual, manual, and cognitive attention simultaneously, tripling the interference. Phone conversations are mainly cognitive-verbal but still impair driving. Texting requires looking away from the road, which phone calls do not, making it far more dangerous.

faq.question: Do hands-free devices make phone use while driving safe?
faq.answer: No. Research consistently shows hands-free phone conversations impair driving almost as much as handheld calls. The danger comes primarily from the cognitive distraction of conversation, not from holding the phone. Hands-free laws address the wrong part of the problem.
